title: United Mine Workers v. Gibbs (1966)
summary: Related federal and state claims could fall within one constitutional case, while the court retained discretion over whether to hear the state claim.
notes:
The historical term “pendent jurisdiction” describes the related state claim in this setting. Do not treat Gibbs alone as resolving the later pendent-party questions in Aldinger, Kroger, and Finley.

Justice Brennan wrote the opinion; the case came from the Eastern District of Tennessee, where a jury found for Gibbs, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed before the Supreme Court granted certiorari. The Court replaced the narrower Hurn v. Oursler test with the 'common nucleus of operative fact' standard, under which the state and federal claims must be ones a plaintiff would ordinarily expect to try in one judicial proceeding.

Despite upholding pendent jurisdiction, the Court reversed the judgment for Gibbs on the merits, so the case is a jurisdictional win and a substantive loss for the plaintiff; pendent jurisdiction was described as a doctrine of discretion, not of plaintiff's right, and state claims should ordinarily be dismissed if the federal claims drop out before trial.

sections.Parties: Gibbs sued the United Mine Workers over interference with his employment and hauling opportunities associated with a mine dispute.
sections.Material Facts: Union activity and violence allegedly caused Gibbs to lose work as a mine superintendent and a related hauling contract. He asserted a federal labor-law claim and a Tennessee interference claim arising from the same general events. The overlap in conduct, witnesses, and proof made trying the claims together a practical possibility, although their legal theories differed.
sections.Procedural History: The litigation produced a verdict and appellate review addressing both jurisdiction and the merits. The Supreme Court articulated the broader pendent-claim framework. Its ultimate disposition also involved substantive labor-law questions; the jurisdictional discussion should not be mistaken for an unconditional approval of every item of recovery.
sections.Issue: When may a federal court hear a state-law claim associated with a substantial federal claim, and must it do so whenever constitutional power exists?
sections.Holding: Power exists when the claims derive from a common nucleus of operative fact and ordinarily would be tried together. Exercise of that power remains discretionary.
sections.Reasoning: The constitutional idea of a “case” need not track the older technical categories of separate causes of action. Factual relationships can justify resolving different legal theories in one proceeding. The Court nevertheless emphasized judicial economy, convenience, fairness, and comity. Early loss of the federal claim, predominance of state issues, difficult state-law questions, and possible jury confusion may support declining or separating claims. The authority to hear a claim and the wisdom of exercising that authority therefore require distinct analysis. Later § 1367 provides the governing statutory structure studied in the course, while retaining much of this conceptual background.

learning.why: Related federal and state claims could fall within one constitutional case, while the court retained discretion over whether to hear the state claim.

topics.cp-supplemental: A common nucleus of operative fact can make federal and state claims one constitutional case.
topics.cp-supplemental-discretion: Having power to hear the related state claim does not require exercising it in every case.
topics.cp-joinder: Procedural permission to combine claims and subject-matter authority remain separate requirements.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Gibbs distinguishes constitutional power over related claims from the discretionary decision whether to hear the state claims, guided by economy, convenience, fairness, and comity.
topics.cp-supplemental-history: Gibbs is the pendent-jurisdiction case whose common-nucleus test and discretion factors were codified in § 1367.
topics.cp-usc-1367: Section 1367(a) and (c) codify the Gibbs power and discretion framework, so exam analysis of the statute starts from Gibbs.

mnemonic.rationale: A mine superintendent and the union
